notes.summary: The indispensable classical Gauduchon and divergence-form Harnack inputs were checked against primary foundations. Neither grants B. Original scalar duality and smooth exact-maximizer uniqueness remain stipulated background.
notes.detailedSummary: Gauduchon's general standard-metric Theorem 2 applies without the Betti-number restriction of his surface Theorem 1. It supplies the smooth positive conformal factor individually, without uniform bounds. The applicable Harnack theorem concerns nonnegative weak solutions of div(A grad u+b u)=0 with uniformly elliptic bounded A and bounded b. It requires neither coefficient derivatives nor a common VMO modulus, and does not impose the maximum-principle sign condition. These hypotheses are verified for the actual equation in n2.
notes.text:
The problem's scalar-duality equality M(F)=exp(-B_0(F)/n), attained maximum, and uniqueness of the original exact maximizing current for smooth F are used as stipulated background. There are no supplied notes whose results are used.

Qualitative conformal existence was checked in Paul Gauduchon, Les métriques standard d'une surface complexe compacte à premier nombre de Betti pair, Astérisque 126 (1985), 129–135, Theorem 2, §3, pp. 132–133, with the standard-metric definition on p. 131. [Primary text](https://numdam.org/item/AST_1985__126__129_0.pdf). Theorem 2 is the general compact almost-complex theorem; the Betti-number assumption belongs to Theorem 1. Its integrable case supplies, for our smooth positive sigma on compact connected complex X of dimension n>=3, a smooth strictly positive rho with dd^c(rho sigma^(n-1))=0, unique up to positive scaling. Normalize by integral rho dV=1. The source's different constant in d^c does not change closedness. No uniform estimate is taken from this theorem.

The original divergence-form Harnack foundation was checked in Neil S. Trudinger, Linear elliptic operators with measurable coefficients, Ann. Scuola Norm. Sup. Pisa, Ser. 3, 27 (1973), 265–308, §5, particularly Corollary 5.2, p. 302. [Primary paper](https://www.numdam.org/article/ASNSP_1973_3_27_2_265_0.pdf). Its bounded strictly uniformly elliptic specialization permits bounded lower-order coefficients.

The precise classical specialization was also checked in Gilbarg–Trudinger, Elliptic Partial Differential Equations of Second Order, 2001 reprint, equations (8.1), (8.5), (8.6), and Theorem 8.20, pp. 177–178, 199. [Authors' theorem and hypotheses](https://djvu.online/file/jxRRleAzbYjsl). For L u=D_i(A_ij D_j u+b_i u)+c_i D_i u+d u, assume measurable coefficients, A xi dot xi>=a_0|xi|^2, bounded matrix entries, and a_0^(-2)(|b|^2+|c|^2)+a_0^(-1)|d|<=kappa^2. A nonnegative W^(1,2) weak solution satisfies sup_(B_r) u<=H inf_(B_r) u when B_(4r) lies in the domain. H depends on dimension, the principal bound divided by a_0, and kappa r. This theorem requires (8.5)–(8.6), not maximum-principle sign condition (8.8).

Our application has real dimension 2n, c=d=0, u=rho smooth and positive, and coordinate balls B_(5r) strictly inside fixed charts. The coefficients and their uniform bounds are reconstructed in n2. No nondivergence adjoint Harnack theorem, Schauder estimate, derivative bound, or automatic VMO assertion is substituted.

Only classical foundations were inspected; no proposed A–D author proof, prior report, private note, sibling manuscript, or full-review packet was consulted. The 1977 C.R. announcement is an attribution, not an inaccessible full text claimed to have been checked; Gauduchon's general theorem in the 1985 primary exposition was checked instead.

notes.summary: B is proved for EVERY smooth v with delta h<=h+dd^c v<=Lambda h. Exterior differentiation cancels the varying third derivatives, producing a uniformly elliptic divergence equation with bounded drift and hence uniform positive bounds for normalized rho.
notes.detailedSummary: Set sigma=h+dd^c v and S=sigma^(n-1). Then d sigma=dh and d^c sigma=d^c h, so d^c S=(n-1)d^c h wedge sigma^(n-2). The Gauduchon equation is exactly d(d^c rho wedge S+rho d^c S)=0. In fixed holomorphic coordinates its flux is A grad rho+b rho, with A real symmetric, delta^(n-1)A_h<=A<=Lambda^(n-1)A_h, and |b|<=K_h Lambda^(n-2). The audited local Harnack theorem applies without coefficient-derivative bounds. A finite connected cover makes the comparison global; integral rho dV=1 then gives H^(-1)<=rho<=H.
notes.text:
Claim B holds with constants depending only on delta,Lambda and fixed geometry, for EVERY smooth real v satisfying delta h<=sigma=h+dd^c v<=Lambda h. Neither a normalization of v nor a bound on its higher derivatives is needed.

Use d^c=i(barpartial-partial)/(4pi), so dd^c=i partial barpartial/(2pi). Complex integrability gives d(dd^c v)=d^c(dd^c v)=0. Therefore
 d sigma=dh,    d^c sigma=d^c h.
For S=sigma^(n-1), with ordinary wedge powers, the graded Leibniz rule yields
 d S=(n-1)dh wedge sigma^(n-2),
 d^c S=(n-1)d^c h wedge sigma^(n-2).
No third derivatives of v occur. Also
 dd^c S=(n-1)dd^c h wedge sigma^(n-2)
 +(n-1)(n-2)dh wedge d^c h wedge sigma^(n-3).
The second sign follows by interchanging two degree-three forms. This last identity is supplemental; the proof needs only d^c S.

The qualitative theorem in n1 supplies smooth positive rho, normalized by integral rho dV=1. Its equation is exactly
 0=dd^c(rho S)=d(d^c rho wedge S+rho d^c S).
In a fixed holomorphic chart, let Omega be the constant positive real coordinate volume. Define A and b by
 iota_(A grad f) Omega=d^c f wedge S,
 iota_b Omega=d^c S.
The identification between vectors and (2n-1)-forms is an isomorphism. Thus the equation becomes
 div(A grad rho+b rho)=0,
with weak form integral (A grad rho+b rho) dot grad phi dx=0 for compactly supported real test functions.

For clarity, define the covector rotation C xi=i(xi^(0,1)-xi^(1,0))/(4pi), so d^c f=C(df). For real covectors xi,eta, the difference xi wedge C eta-eta wedge C xi has only types (2,0) and (0,2). Its wedge with S vanishes. Consequently A is symmetric, and
 xi dot A xi Omega=xi wedge C xi wedge S>0
for xi!=0: xi wedge C xi is a nonzero positive rank-one (1,1)-form.

Let A_h be the same matrix constructed using h^(n-1). Positivity of wedge products gives
 delta^(n-1)h^(n-1)<=S<=Lambda^(n-1)h^(n-1),
and consequently
 delta^(n-1)A_h<=A<=Lambda^(n-1)A_h.
On relatively compact fixed charts, A_h has fixed positive lower and finite upper eigenvalue bounds. Hence a_0 I<=A<=a_1 I uniformly, with a_0,a_1 depending only on delta,Lambda and the fixed atlas and h.

Furthermore d^c S=(n-1)d^c h wedge sigma^(n-2) gives |b|<=b_0<=K_h Lambda^(n-2) in these charts. The volume identification and h are fixed. No derivative of the varying sigma is estimated. In the Harnack notation of n1, take matrix-entry bound sqrt(2n)a_1 and kappa=b_0/a_0, with c=d=0. Each rho is smooth and therefore belongs to W^(1,2) on the relatively compact balls. All Harnack hypotheses are now verified for EVERY family member; no sign of div b is required.

Choose finitely many balls U_j=B_(r_j) covering X, with B_(5r_j) still in their respective charts. Their local Harnack constants have a common bound H_loc>=1. The intersection graph is connected because the balls cover connected X. If there are N balls, an overlap chain comparing a maximum point and a minimum point yields
 max_X rho<=H_loc^N min_X rho.
Set H=H_loc^N. Since dV(X)=1 and integral rho dV=1, min rho<=1<=max rho. Therefore
 H^(-1)<=rho<=H.
This proves B, with c=H^(-1), C=H.

The proof uses the exact relation sigma=h+dd^c v. It does not establish the same bound for arbitrary varying uniformly equivalent Hermitian forms. The lower-mass hypothesis is neither used nor changed. These are mathematical arguments for every n>=3; the finite symbolic diagnostics described in n4 are supplemental.

notes.summary: A and D are proved on the ORIGINAL geometry. The entire smooth bounded-complex-Hessian family is bounded in C^0 supremum norm, and a local bump produces infinitely many distinct normalized NONCONSTANT densities without altering the zero-lower-mass hypothesis.
notes.detailedSummary: With delta=1-epsilon0, Lambda=1+epsilon0 and H_0=h^n/dV, both J_v/H_0 and c_v/c_0 lie between delta^n and Lambda^n. Hence integral exp(F_v)dV=1 and ||F_v-F_0||_infinity<=n log(Lambda/delta). Every datum is smooth; no derivative norm or common VMO modulus is assumed. For a supported smooth w satisfying dd^c w(p)=h(p), and q outside its support, v_t=t(w-sup w) belongs to the family for sufficiently small positive t. The difference F_t(p)-F_t(q)=log(H_0(p)/H_0(q))+n log(1+t) is strictly increasing. Thus all F_t are distinct and at most one is constant.
notes.text:
Fix 0<epsilon0<1, delta=1-epsilon0 and Lambda=1+epsilon0. The ENTIRE specified potential family is
 V_epsilon0={v smooth real: sup_X v=0, -epsilon0 h<=dd^c v<=epsilon0 h}.
Define sigma_v=h+dd^c v, H_0=h^n/dV, c_0=integral h^n, J_v=sigma_v^n/dV, c_v=integral J_v dV, F_v=log(J_v/c_v), and F_0=log(H_0/c_0).

Pointwise matrix comparison gives delta^n<=J_v/H_0<=Lambda^n. Integration gives delta^n<=c_v/c_0<=Lambda^n. Thus J_v,c_v are positive, every F_v is smooth and real, and integral exp(F_v)dV=1. Also
 F_v-F_0=log(J_v/H_0)-log(c_v/c_0),
so
 ||F_v-F_0||_infinity<=n log(Lambda/delta)
 =n log((1+epsilon0)/(1-epsilon0)).
In particular ||F_v||_infinity<=||F_0||_infinity+n log(Lambda/delta). This proves A.

The boundedness topology is the supremum norm on C^0(X,R), although all data are smooth. No compactness in this topology, derivative bound on F_v or sigma_v, higher-derivative bound on v, or common VMO modulus is assumed.

For D, choose a proper coordinate ball, p inside it, and q outside its closure. Choose a real quadratic Q in coordinates centered at p with dd^c Q(p)=h(p). Multiply Q by a real cutoff equal to one near p and supported in the ball, then extend by zero. This produces globally smooth real w with dd^c w(p)=h(p) and dd^c w(q)=0. The quadratic coefficients are scaled to the stipulated dd^c convention.

Compactness gives finite K>=1 with -Kh<=dd^c w<=Kh. For every t in (0,epsilon0/K), let v_t=t(w-sup_X w). Then sup v_t=0 and -epsilon0 h<=dd^c v_t<=epsilon0 h. At the chosen points,
 J_t(p)=(1+t)^n H_0(p),    J_t(q)=H_0(q).
The normalizing scalar cancels, giving
 F_t(p)-F_t(q)=log(H_0(p)/H_0(q))+n log(1+t).
This is strictly increasing. Hence t->F_t is injective; a constant F_t can occur for at most one parameter. Removing that parameter leaves infinitely many, indeed uncountably many, distinct normalized NONCONSTANT logarithmic densities. They are not constant shifts: normalization forces any such shift to vanish, while the two-point difference distinguishes them.

X,h,dV have not changed. This construction works on EVERY original background already assumed to satisfy v_-(h)=0, without asserting existence of such backgrounds. Positive masses within this restricted uniformly positive family do not control the infimum over ALL bounded genuine h-psh potentials. No conclusion v_-(h)>0 follows. D and the required nonvacuity are established.

notes.summary: C and the original sufficient-condition alternative are proved. EVERY original exact maximizer over the ENTIRE specified family has both dnu/dV and k_T uniformly bounded above and below, hence uniformly in critical L^(n/(n-1)). A–D hold; broader continuous families, all tests, near-maximizers and P16 supports remain outside the result.
notes.detailedSummary: Normalize T_v=rho_v sigma_v^(n-1)/a_v, where a_v=integral h wedge rho_v sigma_v^(n-1)=integral rho_v J_v dV by Stokes. The prescribed solution gives B_0(F_v)=log c_v and M(F_v)=c_v^(-1/n). The original trace convention yields Gamma_(F_v)(T_v)=c_v^(-1/n)rho_v J_v/a_v dV, whose mass equals M(F_v), proving exact maximization. Supplied smooth uniqueness identifies EVERY original exact maximizer with T_v. The distinct densities are p_v=dnu/dV=rho_v J_v/a_v and k_T=rho_v J_v^((n-1)/n)/a_v. Uniform bounds for rho and J give explicit positive bounds for both. The nontrivial C^0-bounded family exists on every fixed assumed zero-lower-mass background, so it meets the complete restricted sufficient-condition alternative.
notes.text:
For every v in the full family of n3, write sigma=sigma_v, J=J_v and F=F_v. Let rho be the factor from n2, normalized by integral rho dV=1. Set
 a_v=integral_X h wedge rho sigma^(n-1),
 T_v=(rho/a_v)sigma^(n-1),
 gamma_v=(rho/a_v)^(1/(n-1))sigma.
Then T_v=gamma_v^(n-1), dd^c T_v=0, T_v is smooth strictly positive, and integral h wedge T_v=1. All powers are ordinary wedge powers.

Stokes and dd^c(rho sigma^(n-1))=0 give integral dd^c v wedge rho sigma^(n-1)=0. Consequently
 a_v=integral_X rho sigma^n=integral_X rho J dV.                 (1)
This preserves the ORIGINAL trace normalization.

Check the determinant convention explicitly. For T=gamma^(n-1), let G be the matrix of gamma in an h-unitary frame and s=tr(G^(-1)). Ordinary wedge algebra gives
 beta wedge T=(1/n)tr(B G^(-1))gamma^n,
 tau_T=h wedge T=(s/n)gamma^n,
 P_T=n G^(-1)/s,    tr P_T=n.
Since gamma^n=det(G)h^n,
 det(P_T)^(1/n)tau_T=det(G)^((n-1)/n)h^n.
Therefore the ORIGINAL definition yields
 Gamma_F(T)=exp(F/n)k_T dV,
 k_T=(gamma^n/dV)^((n-1)/n).                                  (2)
There is no remaining n or factorial correction.

The prescribed sigma_v satisfies sigma_v^n=exp(log c_v+F_v)dV. The stipulated scalar background gives
 B_0(F_v)=log c_v,    M(F_v)=c_v^(-1/n).
Equation (2) gives
 k_(T_v)=(rho/a_v)J^((n-1)/n),
 Gamma_(F_v)(T_v)=c_v^(-1/n)(rho/a_v)J dV.
By (1), its mass is c_v^(-1/n)=M(F_v). Thus T_v is an ORIGINAL EXACT maximizing current. Supplied uniqueness for smooth F_v then identifies EVERY ORIGINAL exact maximizing current with T_v. This uses no identification of arbitrary supporting probabilities.

The two ORIGINAL density normalizations are consequently
 p_v=d nu_(T_v,F_v)/dV=rho J/a_v,
 k_(T_v)=rho J^((n-1)/n)/a_v=p_v J^(-1/n).                     (3)
Integral p_v dV=1. The alternative definition also agrees:
 exp(-F_v/n)M(F_v)p_v=(c_v/J)^(1/n)c_v^(-1/n)p_v=J^(-1/n)p_v.

Let H_0=h^n/dV and define fixed positive numbers
 J_-=delta^n min_X H_0,    J_+=Lambda^n max_X H_0.
From n3, J_-<=J_v<=J_+. From n2, H^(-1)<=rho_v<=H for fixed H>=1. Since rho_v dV is a probability, (1) gives J_-<=a_v<=J_+. Therefore, for EVERY family member and EVERY original exact maximizer,
 H^(-1)J_-/J_+ <= d nu_(T,F_v)/dV <= H J_+/J_-,
 H^(-1)J_-^((n-1)/n)/J_+ <= k_T <= H J_+^((n-1)/n)/J_-.
Taking the minimum of the lower constants and maximum of the upper constants gives common c,C>0 for both densities. Dependence is only on epsilon0 and fixed X,h,dV.

With q=n/(n-1) and dV(X)=1, this implies
 ||d nu_(T,F_v)/dV||_(L^q(dV))<=H J_+/J_-,
 ||k_T||_(L^q(dV))<=H J_+^((n-1)/n)/J_-.
Indeed, the stronger L^infinity bounds imply bounds for every finite exponent. This proves C uniformly over the ENTIRE family, rather than merely for one smooth datum.

The explicit sufficient density condition for original S17 is membership in
 {log((h+dd^c v)^n/(c_v dV)): v smooth real, sup v=0,
 -epsilon0 h<=dd^c v<=epsilon0 h}.
All data are smooth; the asserted boundedness topology is C^0 supremum norm with n3's quantitative bound. Only the displayed generating complex-Hessian bounds are imposed. By n3, the same family contains infinitely many distinct normalized nonconstant densities on EVERY fixed original background already satisfying v_-(h)=0. No background is replaced, and no positive-lower-mass conclusion is drawn. Thus A–D establish the complete original restricted sufficient-condition alternative.

No estimate is claimed for all supremum-bounded continuous F, all normalized Gauduchon tests, or near-maximizers. No identification of arbitrary supports or P16 singleton-support conclusion follows here. The full-test endpoint failure and near-maximizer phenomena are compatible with this restricted theorem. The broader unrestricted exact-adjoint question remains outside this result; no literature priority is claimed.
